The Big Question

🤔 You need to store gym kits for 100 students.

Would you create 100 separate variables?

❌ Bad approach: kit1, kit2, kit3... kit100

Chaos. Hard to loop through. Can't easily add more.

✅ Solution: Use a data structure!

kits = ["Alice", "Bob", ..., "Zoe"] — one name, many values.

Arrays (1D)

Think of a row of Post Office Boxes.

# Index:  0      1      2      3
prices = [10.50, 5.00, 20.00, 7.50]
  • Identifier: prices (The Address)
  • Index: 0, 1, 2, 3 (Box Number)
  • Element: 10.50 (The Content)

Warning: Computers count from 0!

Predict the Output

scores = [98, 55, 72, 88, 41]

scores[2]

72

scores[0]

98

scores[-1]

41 (Last item!)

scores[5]

IndexError!

2D Arrays: The Grid

Just like cinema seats. row, then column.

Concept

Col 0Col 1
Row 0AB
Row 1CD

Code

seats = [
  ["A", "B"],
  ["C", "D"]
]
print(seats[1][0]) # "C"

Parallel Arrays

Connecting data using the index.

names = ["Alice", "Bob"]
ages  = [17, 18]

Index 1 represents Bob (Name) AND 18 (Age).

Abstract Data Structures

How we behave vs How we store things.

Stack

Analogy: Pancake Stack 🥞

LIFO: Last In, First Out.

You eat the top pancake first.

Queue

Analogy: Bus Stop Line 🚌

FIFO: First In, First Out.

First person waits longest.

Tracing a Stack

Follow the operations step-by-step.

s = Stack()
s.push(5)
s.push(8)
s.pop()
s.push(3)

Press Down to Trace

1. push(5)

Stack: [5]

2. push(8)

Stack: [5, 8] (8 is top)

3. pop()

Removes top (8).

Stack: [5]

4. push(3)

Adds 3 to top.

Final Stack: [5, 3]

Tracing a Queue

Linear Queue: Join back, Leave front.

q = Queue()
q.enqueue("A")
q.enqueue("B")
q.dequeue()
q.enqueue("C")

Press Down to Trace

1. enqueue("A")

Queue: [A]

2. enqueue("B")

Queue: [A, B]

3. dequeue()

Removes front ("A").

Queue: [B]

4. enqueue("C")

Adds to back ("C").

Final Queue: [B, C]

Static vs Dynamic

Static (The Bus)

Fixed Seats.

Once built, you can't add more seats. Fast to find your seat (index).

Example: Array

Dynamic (The Train)

Add Carriages.

Can grow as needed. Harder to walk to the back.

Example: Linked List / Python List

🧠 Quick Check

State the access order for a Stack.

LIFO — Last In, First Out

State the access order for a Queue.

FIFO — First In, First Out

Misconception Check

A. Arrays always start indexing at 1.

B. A static data structure cannot change size after creation.

C. pop() removes from the bottom of a stack.

D. A 2D array uses [row][column] indexing.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Arrays index from 0 in most languages.

B: True. Static structures have fixed size at creation.

C: False. pop() removes from the TOP (LIFO).

D: True. Row first, then column.

Key Takeaways

  • Arrays store multiple values under one identifier; index from 0.
  • 2D arrays are grids: [row][column].
  • Stacks = LIFO (push/pop); Queues = FIFO (enqueue/dequeue).
  • Static = fixed size; Dynamic = can grow/shrink.
  • Parallel arrays link related data by index position.
